author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
Reviewing AI generated code is not that bad if your harness is built correctly with evidence and reports along the way

Trying to get other people to review your AI generated code is much harder.

It is probably easier for me to just reimplement their code from scratch using AI than trying to use AI to fix their code and get the original owner approve the new AI code.

author.name: Bob Henderson

replies.text:
Horace Chan I'm not talking good or bad code. I'm talking supportable. Even 'bad' code, if it's doing the tasks in the way the business needs it to, is good code if its supportable.

The issue I have is the idea that we just recreate the wheel each time vs focusing on sustainability. Even if we're talking about the waste of pure tokens, restarting every time is hugely inefficient.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Bob Henderson I am not going to throw away my good code. The problem is other people's bad code that I have to support

It is harder to understand and support other people's bad code than use AI to refactor and reimplement their bad code into my good code.

Given that AI can pretty much nail the external behavior of the old code to the wall and rewrite everything inside. Why not just burn some tokens and make your life easier down the road?

Why do you want to support another person's code?  I support my own code, that's what I am paid to do.  If I inherit someone else code, I will morphy it into something that fit my taste so I am willing to support.

The real problem is the original owner of those bad code is still around and I am forced to support their bad code.  They refuse to admit their code is bad

author.name: Bob Henderson
author.headline: Director of Information Technology | Opinions don’t matter more than facts.

replies.text:
Horace Chan There are people against *any* way.

Meritocracy has some pretty well known drawbacks, but the biggest one is the one represented in this post: The hubris of the winners and the tyranny of merit. When the entire system is designed around 'you get what you deserve', those that are 'winning' are known to implement systems that keep them 'winning' while holding back others. It's a self-replicating system, as it becomes the standard and the expectation, so you must keep pushing to be at the top.

From a pure 'productivity is God and number must go up' mindset? Sure, works great. The problem is we're doing this with people, which have different needs, desires, drives, histories, and abilities to input.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Bob Henderson Isn't productivity is God and number must go up is how the business world works?

Even if you don't follow the way, your competitors will, and you will lose marketshare and eventually the company will go bust.  It is the only stable and viable system.

author.name: Bob Henderson
author.headline: Director of Information Technology | Opinions don’t matter more than facts.

replies.text:
Horace Chan This 100% depends on the type of business you're in. Yes, for some, number must go up is the only answer. And if that's what you wanna do, go for it.

But the moment your 'number' involves people, it's a lot harder to quantify. Service driven organizations and such have a much harder time at this. And with AI making 'number must go up' deliverables that much easier to manufacturer, I think we may be seeing a shift towards the harder to quantify, human-driven solutions.

If it works for you, I wish you luck.

Bob Henderson AI works surprisingly well mapping previously hard to quatify stuff into clean numbers that you can optimize for.

Take the messy human out of the equation then you can get some elegant engineering solutions.

author.name: Val Akkapeddi
author.headline: Director of Engineering @ Harbor Health | Hacker | Fountain Pen Enthusiast

comments.text:
I would love to see these claims backed up by actual objectivity.

With the utmost respect - most developers I've worked with in my career don't actually understand what "clean code" is. There are in metrics and theory behind this.

But what most people think it means is "code that I can understand". You will ALWAYS find code that you read or generated "readable", at least short-term. Evidence doesn't necessarily help - unless it plugs into an objective framework - because when you get right down to it, code and prose are both artifacts bouncing off of a mental model. Evidence that you generated will look more readable to you too.

The phenomenon you're describing - people rewriting other people's AI generated code with AI code - is specifically the problem I have to solve as a manager of ICs, because it leads to dilution of signal.

Maybe each individual developer's input is more comprehensible to them, and their individual definition of done looks complete, but it rots maintainability & provability at an actual product level.

And I'm not bad enough to coding to perform fake humility and defer to ICs and accept churn as the cost of doing business, sorry.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Val Akkapeddi You got it.  It is the human understanding of the real thing that matters,  code is just one of the manifest.

With AI, code is just an artifact, the harness, agent, whatever you call it that generate the code is the primary work surface.

Divide and conquer is the only way, a single brain somewhere should know how all piece are connected, then each level of abstraction or detail should have a brain that knows it inside out.

Problem of modern system is NO ONE actually know what's going on inside.
